meta.title: Deep Learning
meta.mystery: What becomes possible when a neural network can build on its own earlier representations?

arrive.title: At what point does a collection of pixels become a "7"?
arrive.body1: A neural network doesn't receive the idea of a “7.” It receives numerical information from the pixels.
arrive.body2: So how does that information become something the network can use to recognize a 7?

compose.title: Each step builds on the last
compose.body: This is the same 7 from a moment ago. Stack a couple of changes — like layering one photo filter on top of another — and watch each new one work on the result of the step before it, not the original.
compose.gateHint: Add at least two to see it.
compose.pivot: You just picked those steps yourself. What if the network could work out its own — and far more useful ones?

compressHuman.title: Describe this 7 using only 20 numbers
compressHuman.body: Imagine describing this 7 to someone over the phone so they can redraw it — but all you're allowed to send is 20 numbers. Set each value to anything you like and watch what gets drawn from them. Then see the 20 numbers the network chose.
compressHuman.liveHelper: Drag any slider — the drawing updates as you go.
compressHuman.takeaway: Anyone can pick 20 numbers. But these 20 were learned from the image, so they contain enough information for the network to rebuild the 7.

compressBottleneck.title: What if you get even fewer numbers?
compressBottleneck.body: A moment ago the network summed up this 7 in 20 numbers. Now change how many numbers it's allowed to use, and watch how much of the 7 still comes back.
compressBottleneck.scaleHint: more numbers → more detail · fewer numbers → less detail

readout.5: 5 numbers: only the rough shape of the 7 survives.
readout.20: 20 numbers: still clearly a 7, some detail lost.
readout.100: 100 numbers: nearly all the detail comes back.

compressBottleneck.takeaway: The fewer numbers it's allowed, the less of the 7 can survive. It keeps the big shape and drops the fine detail first.

compressReveal.title: Those 20 numbers have a name: a representation
compressReveal.definition: A representation captures something in a way that keeps the information that’s useful and leaves out the rest.
compressReveal.analogy: Like a map captures the important features of a place without showing every detail, or a summary captures the main ideas of a long article.
compressReveal.recap: You couldn't sum up the 7 in 20 numbers by hand. The network could — not in words, but as 20 numbers that hold enough to redraw it.
compressReveal.tease: So what gets kept, and what gets dropped, when there's very little room?

deepenCallback.title: Layers build on one another
deepenCallback.body1: Each layer takes the representation from the layer before it and transforms it into a new one.
deepenCallback.body2: Researchers often find that these layers develop increasingly complex patterns after training. But this is something we observe in the trained network — it isn’t a set of rules the network was given.

deepenInspect.title: What can more steps do?
deepenInspect.body: Set the 7 aside for one screen — this puzzle shows the idea more clearly. Each dot is one of two colours, and the network has to draw a line that puts one colour on each side.
deepenInspect.shallowResult: Few steps: the line stays straight — and can't separate them. Gets it right {pct}% of the time.
deepenInspect.deeperResult: More steps: the line can bend and wrap around — now it separates them. Right {pct}% of the time.
deepenInspect.takeaway: This is Lesson 5's Impossible Split again: one straight line can't do it. More steps let the network bend the line into a shape that can. That's what depth buys — not "smarter," just able to handle trickier shapes.
deepenInspect.training: Training the shallow and deeper nets…
deepenInspect.cta: Couldn't you just add more units? →

deepenWidth.title: Couldn't you just add more units instead?
deepenWidth.body: Depth helped on that puzzle. But here's the obvious objection — instead of stacking layers, why not keep one layer and pack in more units? Same number of parts, either way. Lay them out wide, or stack them deep. Try both on the same dots.
deepenWidth.predictLabel: Your guess: will more units in one layer separate the dots?
deepenWidth.predictFirst: Predict first, then try both layouts.
deepenWidth.illustrativeNote: Illustrative — same {n} units either way (one wide layer vs three stacked).

readout.wide: One wide layer, {n} units: the line still can't bend — {pct}% right. More width didn't buy the bend.
readout.deep: The same {n} units in a few layers: the line wraps around the dots — {pct}% right.

deepenWidth.takeaway: More units in one layer is not the same as more layers. With the same number of parts, stacking them into steps lets each step reshape what the last one did — so the boundary can bend and wrap in ways one wide layer can't. Depth isn't "more neurons." It's parts that build on each other.
deepenWidth.hedge: A single layer can, in principle, fit almost any shape — if you make it wide enough. The catch is that "wide enough" can mean absurdly, impractically wide. Stacking is how you get the same power at a workable size. Depth trades width for order.

deepenPlateau.title: Does more always help?
deepenPlateau.body: You just saw that adding depth helped. So here’s the natural next question: if some depth helps, does adding more and more always make the network better?
deepenPlateau.chartTitle: How well it does, by depth
deepenPlateau.chartSummaryTemplate: Rises to depth {peak}, then falls — more depth stopped helping.

readout.worse: Depth {d}: {pct}% — worse, and harder to train.
readout.shallow: Depth {d}: {pct}% — too shallow, can't bend enough.

deepenPlateau.reveal: More depth isn't automatically better. Past a point, extra layers stop helping and start hurting — they get harder to train, and the model does worse. Depth is an opportunity, not a guarantee.

deepenReveal.title: Depth is an opportunity, not a guarantee
deepenReveal.body1: More layers give a network more room to learn — but they also make training harder. Extra depth isn’t automatically better.
deepenReveal.historyCallback: As you saw in Lesson 5, some patterns are too complex for a single layer. Adding layers makes more transformations possible.
deepenReveal.historyNew: Stacking alone wasn’t enough. Training methods had to improve too. In 2012, AlexNet showed what was possible when depth met workable training, data, and compute.
deepenReveal.whyBody: ImageNet was a large benchmark for recognizing objects in images. AlexNet’s breakthrough there helped show that large, deep networks could work remarkably well once the training methods, data, and computing were ready.

tracker.title: Before and after
tracker.before: Neural networks have layers and adjustable parameters.
tracker.after: Deep learning uses multiple layers of learned transformations to construct useful representations from data.

closing.title: You just saw what happens when a network can build on one transformation after another.
closing.question: But what does the network actually learn to represent?
closing.hint: Data and a task — without being told which features to look for. So where do those useful features come from?

challenge.correct: Correct — composed transformations and useful representations.
challenge.wrong: Not quite. Remember wide vs deep — more units in one layer couldn't bend the line; stacking the same units could. Depth is composed transformations, not more neurons or “thinking harder.” Try again.

seoSpine.lead: Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers so the system can build richer internal representations — from simple patterns to more abstract ones — by stacking transformations.

sections.heading: Why are neural networks deep?
sections.body: Depth lets each stage reuse what earlier layers already computed. A shallow model often hits a wall; a deeper stack can compose many small computations into more flexible behavior.

sections.heading: What do layers learn in deep learning?
sections.body: Earlier layers often latch onto simpler structure. Later layers combine those responses into higher-level features. That progression is a big part of what “deep learning explained” really means.
